_meta.description: Mapping of finding types to the five Cyber Essentials control themes. Cyber Essentials is the UK government's baseline cyber security certification, required by many public-sector contracts. The scheme has five technical control themes: Firewalls, Secure Configuration, User Access Control, Malware Protection, and Security Update Management.
_meta.mapping_rationale: Cyber Essentials themes are broad. Cloud misconfigurations typically touch Secure Configuration (the default and most-used theme for cloud) and User Access Control (when the misconfiguration affects who can access data). Mappings below reflect the primary theme(s) each finding directly compromises.

audit_notes.S3_PUBLIC_VIA_ACL: Two themes. User Access Control is primary — an AllUsers grant is a direct failure of access control. Secure Configuration is secondary — the bucket was configured insecurely at creation or through subsequent changes.
audit_notes.S3_PUBLIC_ACCESS_BLOCK_DISABLED: Secure Configuration only. PAB is a bucket-level configuration setting; the theme covers exactly this case.
audit_notes.S3_ENCRYPTION_DISABLED: Secure Configuration only. Encryption at rest is a default AWS bucket configuration; a bucket without it has been configured (or left configured) insecurely.
audit_notes.S3_VERSIONING_DISABLED: Secure Configuration only. Cyber Essentials has no dedicated backup or resilience theme, so this is mapped to the same theme as the other S3 findings: versioning is a bucket-level configuration setting, and its absence is a configuration gap rather than a control from a different theme.
audit_notes.S3_LOGGING_DISABLED: Secure Configuration only, for the same reason as versioning: Cyber Essentials has no monitoring or logging theme in its five-theme baseline, so this is the nearest fit rather than a precise one.
audit_notes.S3_LIFECYCLE_MISSING: Secure Configuration only. No retention-specific theme exists in the five-theme baseline; a lifecycle policy is a bucket-level configuration setting, so this is the same nearest-fit reasoning as the other two.
audit_notes.S3_TLS_NOT_ENFORCED: Secure Configuration only. A bucket policy enforcing TLS is a configuration setting, same as the other S3 findings; Cyber Essentials' baseline does not separate transit encryption into its own theme.
audit_notes.KMS_KEY_ROTATION_DISABLED: Secure Configuration only. Key rotation is a configuration setting on the key, same reasoning as every other finding in this file; Cyber Essentials has no cryptography-specific theme.
audit_notes.KMS_KEY_PENDING_DELETION: Secure Configuration only, for lack of a better theme. This finding is really an operational/incident-response matter more than a configuration one, but Cyber Essentials' five-theme baseline has no closer fit.
audit_notes.IAM_ROOT_ACCESS_KEYS_ACTIVE: User Access Control, primary this time rather than secondary as it was for S3_PUBLIC_VIA_ACL. Root credential management is squarely what this theme covers.
audit_notes.IAM_ACCOUNT_MFA_NOT_ENABLED: User Access Control, reused. MFA is a core expectation of this theme — Cyber Essentials' own guidance explicitly names MFA as part of what User Access Control means in practice.
audit_notes.IAM_PASSWORD_POLICY_WEAK: User Access Control, reused again. Cyber Essentials' own technical requirements for this theme explicitly include password-based authentication standards, so this is as direct a fit as the other three IAM findings.
audit_notes.IAM_ACCESS_KEY_AGE_EXCEEDS_90_DAYS: User Access Control, fifth use. Credential rotation and removal of stale access is one of the theme's core expectations, alongside strong passwords and MFA.
